name: Blackburne's Mate
summary: Two bishops and a knight combine to mate a castled king on g8: the light bishop lands on h7, the knight guards it, and the long diagonal is sealed
intro: Blackburne's Mate is an attacking checkmate that harnesses two bishops and a knight against a castled king. A light-squared bishop lands on h7 next to the king, a knight defends it so the king cannot capture, and a dark-squared bishop rakes the long diagonal to cut off every escape. Named for the nineteenth-century English master Joseph Henry Blackburne, it is shown here in the diagram with White's pieces perfectly coordinated for a one-move finish against the king on g8.
boardCaption: White to move: the light bishop swings from d3 to h7, mating the king on g8, defended by the g5 knight and backed by the b2 bishop.

sections.heading: What Blackburne's Mate is
paragraphs: Blackburne's Mate is a coordinated checkmate that uses three minor pieces: two bishops and a knight. The light-squared bishop delivers the check by landing right beside the king, the knight supports that bishop so it cannot be captured, and the dark-squared bishop sweeps the long diagonal to seize the escape squares behind the king. Together the three pieces build a net around a king that has castled into the corner.

In this position every piece is in place. White's light bishop stands on d3, aimed along the b1-h7 diagonal at the king on g8. The knight sits on g5, and the dark bishop is planted on b2 controlling the long a1-h8 diagonal. The black king has castled and is sheltered only by the rook on f8, with no kingside pawns left in front of it, exactly the exposed setup this mate is designed to punish.

sections.heading: The mating move
paragraphs: White plays Bh7#, moving the light-squared bishop from d3 to h7 to check the king on g8 from the neighbouring square. The king cannot take the bishop, because the knight on g5 guards h7. Since the check is delivered from an adjacent square, there is no way to interpose a piece to block it either, so the king must try to run.

But the flight squares are all covered. The bishop on b2 rakes the long diagonal through f6 and g7 to h8, so both g7 and the corner square h8 are denied to the king. The knight on g5 additionally controls f7, removing that escape as well. The king's only other square, f8, is occupied by its own rook. With capture, interposition, and every flight cut off, Bh7 is checkmate.

sections.heading: How to use it
paragraphs: Aim for Blackburne's Mate when the enemy king has castled kingside and its pawn shield has been stripped away. The key is coordination: place a knight where it guards the h7 square, put your dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal to control g7 and h8, and then deliver with the light-squared bishop on h7. Check that the mating bishop is protected and that the king's escape to f7 and the long diagonal are both sealed before committing.

As the defender, treat an open king with an enemy knight near g5 and a bishop on the long diagonal as a serious alarm. Keeping pawns in front of the castled king, or blunting the long diagonal with a piece of your own, denies the attacker the squares this mate depends on. Once all three white pieces are trained on the corner as in the diagram, the mate cannot be stopped, so the defence must come earlier.

keyIdeas: Blackburne's Mate combines two bishops and a knight against a castled king.
The light-squared bishop mates on h7 right next to the king on g8.
The knight on g5 defends h7, so the king cannot capture the bishop.
The dark-squared bishop on b2 covers g7 and h8 along the long diagonal.
The knight also guards f7, and the king's own rook blocks f8.
Prepare it against a castled king whose pawn cover has been removed.
